archetype.name: Bubble Team (goalie-carried)
archetype.definition: Nashville has a playoff-pace record built on Juuse Saros and a league-best penalty kill, while its 5-on-5 play sits in the bottom third, so its place in the standings depends on that goaltending and that kill holding up.

report.headline: Saros and a 90% kill are covering for a team that gets outshot
report.take:
Nashville is 11-5-5, fourth in a crowded Central, 11th on the site, and on pace for 105 points. Read the standings alone and this looks like a clean bounce-back from last year's 86-point team. The underlying profile is something different. At 5-on-5 the Predators take only 46% of the shot attempts (28th) and 48.4% of the expected goals (21st). They allow 28.4 shots a game, 24th in the league. This is a team that spends a lot of its even-strength time defending.

Two things are covering that up. The first is Saros: .917, 9.4 goals saved above expected, fifth on the goalie tab, with the team's 12.4 GSAx second in the league. The second is special teams. The power play converts 26.1% (7th), with Stamkos, O'Reilly and Josi each past ten power-play points. The penalty kill sits at 90%, first in the league and well above a league average around 77%. Those two levers explain how a team ranked 21st in scoring holds a 6th-ranked defense and a positive goal differential (+5).

The month split tells the story. October went 5-9 with 3.36 goals allowed a game. November is 6-1 with 1.71 allowed, and that run included a seven-game winning streak. The scoring barely moved between the two months, at 3.00 and then 3.14 a game. Everything changed in the net and on the kill, while the shot shares stayed poor, and several of the streak's wins came in overtime. History is a warning here too. In 2022-23 this franchise posted 61.5 GSAx with a 47.7% xGF share and finished with 92 points and no playoff wins.

The team is not a mirage. The top of the lineup is legitimate: Forsberg (23 points, +10, 52% xGF), Stamkos (12 goals), and Josi logging nearly 26 minutes with 23 points. The defense also holds opposing wingers well below their norms. But the blueline behind Josi grades C-, and the third and fourth centers are being outchanced. Expect the 90% kill and the November goals-against rate to come back toward normal, and the record to settle into bubble territory rather than division-title territory.

strengths.title: Saros is stealing goals
strengths.body: Saros has saved 9.4 goals above expected in 15 starts and ranks fifth among the league's goalies, and the team's GSAx is second overall. Nashville's all-situations save percentage of .910 is well above the league's .892, and that gap is most of why a team allowing the 24th-most shots ranks 6th in goals against. Saros has track record enough to stay good, but a GSAx this high over a full season is rare even for elite goalies.

strengths.title: Special teams winning games
strengths.body: The penalty kill at 90% leads the league by a distance, and the power play at 26.1% is top-ten. The power play looks repeatable: it is driven by Stamkos, O'Reilly and Josi, who carry real finishing and distribution. The kill is partly a goaltending product and will drift down, though last season's 81.7% shows it was already a solid unit.

strengths.title: Top-line skill and wingers shut down
strengths.body: Forsberg and Josi are both top-ten at their positions on the site and are among the few regulars on the right side of the chance share. Without the puck, Nashville holds opposing wingers almost a full point a game under their expected output, second-best in the league. That gives the defense a real base beyond the goalie.

concerns.title: Losing the 5-on-5 territory battle
concerns.body: A 46% Corsi share (28th) and a 48.4% xGF share (21st) are not playoff-team numbers. The team is getting outshot on most nights. Those shares are worse than last year's, when the team sat at an even 50% of the shot attempts. If Saros merely becomes good rather than great, the goals-against rank will slide toward the middle of the league.

concerns.title: November defense won't hold
concerns.body: Nashville allowed 1.71 goals a game in November and 1.80 over its last five, against 3.36 in October. The shot volume did not fall enough to explain that drop. The all-situations PDO of 102.2 is above the league's 100.6, and the improvement came from saves and kills, not suppression. Some of that November gain will give back.

concerns.title: Thin blueline and bottom six
concerns.body: Behind Josi and Wilsby the defense grades C-. Skjei, Perbix and Struble are all under 45% xGF while playing real minutes. Up front, Bourque has no goals on 34 shots and a 39.8% xGF share in 16 minutes a night. The depth is where the chance share bleeds.

trend.note: A 5-9 October turned into a 6-1 November, including a seven-game win streak that ended in San Jose. The surge came almost entirely from goals against, not from controlling play.

weekAhead.headline: A measuring stick in Minnesota, then a dangerous Pittsburgh at home
weekAhead.body:
Only two games this week, and they point in opposite directions. Tuesday in Minnesota is the hardest test in the division. The Wild are 15-3-4 and second on the site. They lead the league in fewest goals allowed, rank first in GSAx and save percentage, and hold forwards further under their norms than anyone. Nashville's even-strength game is unlikely to win a territorial battle here, so its best path is the power play. Minnesota's kill is only 14th at 79.4%, which gives Nashville's top-seven power play a real opening.

Saturday's visit from Pittsburgh looks soft on paper at 7-11-2 and 24th on the site. The Penguins are better than that. They win 52.4% of the expected goals and 52% of the attempts, both better than Nashville, and their record is dragged down by an .882 save percentage and the third-worst Pts vs Goal Diff. That makes it a game where Nashville is likely to be outplayed again and where its own goaltending edge should decide it. Pittsburgh's wingers and forwards concede points freely, which sets up well for Forsberg and the top line.

keyMatchups.title: Nashville power play vs Wild kill
keyMatchups.body: Minnesota allows almost nothing at even strength and ranks first in holding forwards under expectation. Its penalty kill is middle-of-the-pack, though, while Nashville's power play converts 26.1%. Drawing penalties may be the only reliable route to offense in that game.

keyMatchups.title: Saros vs Pittsburgh's shot volume
keyMatchups.body: Pittsburgh outchances opponents and then loses on goaltending. Nashville is the opposite. If the Penguins push the play as their 52.4% xGF suggests, the gap between Saros and a Pittsburgh crease saving only .882 decides the night.

keyMatchups.title: Forsberg against leaky Penguin wings
keyMatchups.body: Pittsburgh gives wingers 0.6 points a game more than their norms, 26th in the league against forwards overall. Forsberg, the team's best play-driver among forwards, is the obvious beneficiary.

weekAhead.watch: Shots against in Minnesota: if Nashville again gives up far more than it creates and still gets points, that is Saros, not a team that has turned a corner.

restOfSeason.body: The 105-point pace will not survive. A league-leading 90% kill, a November goals-against rate near 1.7, and a GSAx this high are the parts most likely to regress. The 46% Corsi share is the part most likely to persist. What is sustainable is a top-heavy offense with a good power play, real goaltending, and solid work against opposing wingers. That profile resembles a .530-.560 points team over the rest of the way, which lands Nashville around the low 90s. In this Central, that means a wild-card fight rather than a division race. Annunen's .886 in five starts also matters: every night Saros rests is a night the team's main edge disappears.
swingFactors: Whether the 5-on-5 shot share climbs toward 50%
Depth defense behind Josi and Wilsby

confidence.note: 21 games; shot shares are stable, but PK and save % samples are small.
